abstract: |
  Every copy-number caller writes its results in its own layout, often spread
  over several files and with differently named fields. `cnvstrmliner` provides
  one parser per supported caller, all returning the same `cnvstrml` object.
  This vignette runs five callers -- FACETS, SCLUST, PureCN, Sequenza and
  Control-FREEC -- over the same whole-exome sample, shows the quirks of each
  output, and then uses the common representation to plot the callers side by
  side, build a consensus and compare a parameter sweep at cohort level.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(cnvstrmliner)
library(logger)
library(GenomicRanges)
library(ggplot2)
library(DT)
log_threshold(level = WARN, namespace = "cnvstrmliner")
```

# Introduction

The proliferation of Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) tools for predicting 
Copy Number Aberrations (CNAs) has led to a significant data integration 
challenge in bioinformatics. Each application, while serving the same core purpose, 
generates results in a unique output format, often spread across multiple files. 
Furthermore, the specific metrics and fields reported—such as segment start/end positions, 
log-ratio values, and associated p-values—are frequently named differently or 
are not uniformly present across all tool outputs. 
This lack of standardization creates substantial overhead for researchers, 
who must write custom parsing scripts for every new tool, leading to complex 
and error-prone downstream analysis. It is exceptionally difficult to compare 
results across different methods, integrate them into common analysis pipelines, 
or use them with existing visualization and interpretation software, 
even when using semi-standard formats like SEG or VCF which haven't achieved universal adoption.

A dedicated package capable of reading the diverse outputs of CNA prediction tools 
and translating them into a single, common, standardized format is crucial for 
streamlining genomic data analysis. Such a package would significantly reduce 
the need for custom scripting, allowing researchers to focus on biological 
interpretation rather than data wrangling. By providing a consistent data 
structure, it would immediately enable method comparison, consensus calling, 
and seamless integration with downstream analysis and visualization tools, 
irrespective of the initial prediction method. This unified approach promotes 
reproducibility and interoperability across different studies and laboratories, 
ultimately accelerating the pace of discovery in cancer genomics and other fields 
relying on CNA analysis.

`cnvstrmliner` is a package that tries to assume the role of this middle layer
that is capable of parsing multiple output formats and provide a single uniform one 
using standard Bioconductor objects.
Furthermore, some additional functionality is added to facilitate the comparisons and 
QC.

## The example dataset

Every example in this vignette uses a single sample, **`BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T`**, that
ships with the package under `extdata/example_CNV/BRCA_XX_01`. It is a simulated
breast tumour / matched normal pair diluted to a nominal 30% tumour purity, processed
through five different CNV callers. Because all the results describe the *same*
underlying sample, it is well suited for showing both how the individual
parsers work and how the results of different callers can be compared, merged and
plotted side by side.

The sample is **whole-exome (WES)**, captured with the Agilent SureSelect Human All Exon
V6 kit; the target coordinates ship next to the caller output as
`S07604514_Regions_v6_hg38_Targets.bed`. This is worth keeping in mind when reading the
plots below: the callers only observe the captured intervals, so breakpoints are pinned to
target boundaries, segments carry far fewer markers than they would in WGS, and long
stretches between targets are interpolated rather than measured. It is also part of why
the callers disagree as much as they do on this sample.

```{r datadir}
root <- system.file("extdata/example_CNV/BRCA_XX_01", package = "cnvstrmliner")
list.dirs(root, recursive = FALSE, full.names = FALSE)
```

The `getSupportedMethods()` function lists the callers that the package knows how to read.

```{r supported}
getSupportedMethods()
```

Typically, for each supported caller the function `loadCNV()` can be used to load data,
using the `cnv.method` argument to specify the caller.
There is also a `parse<CALLER>` function that loads the data by parsing the usual files
produced by the caller (in fact `loadCNV()` is a dispatch function that calls the
appropriate `parse<CALLER>` function).

The result is a `cnvstrml` object that contains several slots with related information.
Notably, `cnvObj@segments` contains a `GRanges` object with all the segments and their
annotation.

The annotation of this `GRanges` object is uniform and contains the `total.allele.copies`,
`major.allele.copies`, `minor.allele.copies` etc as well as the `ccf` and `cf` of each
segment. If the method provides subclones (e.g. Battenberg or SCLUST) it also provides the
copies of Clone1 and Clone2.

In all cases the column `total.allele.copies` contains the total copies in a segment,
`major.allele.copies` the major allele copies and 
`minor.allele.copies` contains the minor allele copies
(`total.allele.copies = minor.allele.copies + major.allele.copies`).
`cnv.loh` is a flag (TRUE/FALSE) indicating if a segment has lost its heterozygosity. 
In combination with `cnv.annotation`, which contains the type of event (NEUT, AMP, DEL, LOH etc),
it provides a uniform way to annotate segments.
Additionally, when the method provides it, `cnv.cf` and `cnv.ccf` contain the cell fraction (purity)
and cancer cell fraction respectively.
Finally, if the method provides it, the logR of the segment is stored in the `cnv.lrr` column.
After QC metrics have been applied the segments also contain the `cnv.cnaqc.pass` flag
indicating if the segment passed the CNAqc test or not.

Other slots include `cnvObj@purity` with the purity estimated by the method, 
`cnvObj@ploidy` with the ploidy (which can be a float number) and 
`cnvObj@effective_ploidy` with the ploidy of the majority of the genome (integer).


# Load and parse data from various callers

## FACETS

FACETS reports its segmentation in a single VCF file, with purity and ploidy stored in the
VCF header. `parseFACETS()` accepts either that VCF (plain, bgzipped or `.bgz`) or a
`data.frame` with the segment table.

```{r facets}
facets.file <- file.path(
  root, "FACETS",
  "BRCA_XX_01_normal_wg-BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T.vcf.gz"
)

facets <- parseFACETS(facets.file, sample = "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T", genome = "hg38")
facets
```

Printing the object gives the purity/ploidy estimated by the caller, the inferred sex and
whatever quality information could be recovered from the caller's own output. The
harmonised segments live in the `segments` slot:

```{r facets_segments}
head(facets@segments, 3)
```

Note that alongside the columns produced by FACETS itself (`TCN_EM`, `LCN_EM`, `CF_EM`, ...)
the parser has added the uniform `total.allele.copies` / `major.allele.copies` /
`minor.allele.copies` / `cnv.annotation` / `cnv.loh` / `cnv.ccf` set that every other
parser in the package produces as well.

### Plotting a single sample

`plotSegments()` gives a visual overview of the genome. Segments are coloured by
`cnv.annotation` and the dotted horizontal line marks the effective ploidy of the sample.

```{r facets_plot}
plotSegments(facets)
```

The same function accepts a number of arguments that change what is shown.
`chromosomes` restricts the plot to a subset of the genome, and `main` / `subtitle`
override the automatically generated labels.

```{r facets_plot_chrom}
#| fig.width: 7
plotSegments(
  facets,
  chromosomes = c("chr1", "chr6", "chr16"),
  main = "BRCA_XX_01 - FACETS",
  subtitle = "Chromosomes 1, 6 and 16"
)
```

`max.copies` caps the y axis (the underlying values are not modified, only the
visualisation), which is useful when a handful of high-level amplifications would
otherwise flatten the rest of the profile. `tiny.segment.frac` controls the size below
which a segment is drawn as a diamond marker rather than a rectangle, so that focal events
remain visible at genome scale.

```{r facets_plot_maxcopies}
plotSegments(facets, max.copies = 10, tiny.segment.frac = 0.002)
```

Finally, `highlightgr` shades a set of regions of interest across the plot. It accepts
either a plain `GRanges`

A single gene locus is only a few tens of kilobases wide, which at chromosome scale is
thinner than the line used to draw it. Padding each region by 1 Mb on either side makes
the shaded band wide enough to see without moving it away from the gene.

```{r facets_plot_highlight}
# ERBB2 and TP53 loci (hg38), padded by 1 Mb upstream and downstream so that the
# highlighted bands are visible at chromosome scale.
pad <- 1e6

roi <- GRanges(
  seqnames = c("chr17", "chr17"),
  ranges = IRanges(
    start = c(39687914, 7668402) - pad,
    end   = c(39730426, 7687550) + pad
  ),
  gene = c("ERBB2", "TP53")
)

plotSegments(facets, highlightgr = roi, chromosomes = "chr17")
```

`highlightgr` also accepts another `cnvstrml` object, in which case the segments of that
object are shaded behind the profile of the first one — a quick way of overlaying the
calls of a second method.


## SCLUST

SCLUST distributes its results over several files (`*_cn_summary.txt`,
`*_allelic_states.txt`, `*_subclonal_cn.txt`, ...). Only one of them has to be given:
the parser derives the common stem and collects all the files it needs.

`r CRANpkg("logger")` can be used to define the level of logging information one wants to see while
this happens.

```{r sclust}
# show what the parser is doing
logger::log_threshold(logger::DEBUG, namespace = "parser")

sclust.file <- file.path(root, "SCLUST", "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T_cn_summary.txt")

sclust <- parseSCLUST(sclust.file, genome = "hg38")

# back to a quiet threshold
logger::log_threshold(logger::WARN, namespace = "parser")

sclust
```

The sample name did not have to be supplied here — SCLUST records it in its summary file
and the parser picks it up.

### Subclones

SCLUST may report two subclones per segment. `updateSCLUSTClone()` builds a new
`cnvstrml` object in which the copy numbers of the requested clone replace the consensus
ones, so the two clonal solutions can be inspected as if they were separate samples.

```{r sclust_clones}
#| fig.height: 8
cloneA <- updateSCLUSTClone(sclust, clone = "Clone1")
cloneB <- updateSCLUSTClone(sclust, clone = "Clone2")

plotSegments(list(sclust, cloneA, cloneB))
```

When `plotSegments()` is given a *list* of objects it stacks the panels and collects a
single shared legend. With three panels or fewer each panel keeps its own title and
subtitle; with more than three the titles are replaced by a compact
`sample` / `method (purity)` label in the left gutter (see the cross-caller comparison
further down).

### Chromosome arm annotation

`addChromosomeAnnotation()` adds the chromosome arm to every segment and splits any
segment that spans a centromere into its p and q parts. Telomeres are typically not
covered by the CNV algorithms, so the annotated object may contain slightly more segments
than the original one.

```{r addchromosomeannotation}
sclust.annot <- addChromosomeAnnotation(sclust)

table(sclust.annot@segments$arm)
```

### Comparing two objects segment by segment

`compareSegmentStatus()` intersects the segments of two `cnvstrml` objects and reports,
for every overlapping interval, the status, the total copy number and the CCF of each
side. Here we compare the two SCLUST subclones.

```{r comparesegments}
comp <- compareSegmentStatus(cloneA, cloneB)

head(comp$table)
```

The last three columns hold the flags `status`, `cnv` and `ccf`, indicating whether the two
segments agree. For the last two columns a value of `SAME` means that although the total
copies and/or the CCF are identical, the *status* is not — e.g.

```
chr1  50596099  85708305   NEUT   HETDEL   2   2   0.25   0.25   FP   SAME   SAME
```

The `summary` and `stats` elements aggregate the same information per karyotype pair and
per status:

```{r comparesegments_stats}
comp$stats
```


## PureCN

PureCN is popular because it can be run against a panel of normals and therefore works
with unmatched tumour samples. Like SCLUST it writes several files sharing a common stem
(`*.csv`, `*_loh.csv`, `*_variants.csv`, `*_genes.csv`), and again a single one of them is
enough to get started.

```{r purecn}
purecn.file <- file.path(root, "PureCN_TCGAref", "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T_loh.csv")

purecn <- parsePureCN(purecn.file, genome = "hg38")
purecn
```

PureCN reports non-integer copy numbers, so the parser warns that the CNV annotations were
derived after rounding; the original `C` and `M` values are kept in the segment metadata
for reference.

```{r purecn_plot}
plotSegments(purecn)
```

`summaryTable()` aggregates the segments by karyotype and event type. It can be run at the
genome, chromosome or arm level.

```{r purecn_summary}
summaryTable(purecn, level = "genome")
```


## Sequenza

Sequenza also writes a directory of files around a common stem; `parseSequenza()` reads
the segments together with the run information, the confidence intervals of the
cellularity/ploidy grid search and the alternative solutions it considered.

```{r sequenza}
sequenza.file <- file.path(root, "Sequenza", "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T_segments.txt")

sequenza <- parseSequenza(sequenza.file, genome = "hg38")
sequenza
```

This particular run is heavily fragmented compared with the other callers, which makes it
a good illustration of the fragmentation test below.

```{r sequenza_plot}
plotSegments(sequenza)
```

### Chromosome overfragmentation

Following the example of CNAqc (which is embedded in the package) one can compute a
p-value for each chromosome arm and test whether the arm is overfragmented.
This version of the function does not require initialising a CNAqc object and allows a
short segment to be defined by its size rather than as a percentage of the chromosome arm.

```{r overfragmentation}
sequenza <- detectOverfragmentation(sequenza)

subset(sequenza@quality$fragmentation$table, significant == TRUE) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  DT::datatable()
```

Passing `arm_percentage_cutoff` as an absolute number of base pairs counts only segments
shorter than that as "short", which usually removes most of the significant arms.

```{r overfragmentation_bp}
sequenza <- detectOverfragmentation(sequenza, arm_percentage_cutoff = 30000000)

subset(sequenza@quality$fragmentation$table, significant == TRUE) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  DT::datatable()
```


## Control-FREEC

Control-FREEC results are distributed over multiple files as well (`*_CNVs`,
`*_info.txt`, `*_ratio.txt`, `*_BAF.txt`). `cnvstrmliner` finds all the necessary files
and compiles the final result: only one of them has to be named. The example data holds
the tumour/normal run of the sample.

```{r cfreec}
freec.file <- file.path(
  root, "ControlFREEC_tn",
  "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T.mpileup.gz_ploidy2_CNVs"
)

freec <- parseCfreec(freec.file, sample = "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T", genome = "hg38")
freec
```

Control-FREEC output contains only the regions of the chromosome that deviate from
neutral. As a result the parser adds the missing segments, but issues a warning to inform
the user about this. It adds the column `cnv.fill` to indicate that a segment was added
through that process.

```{r cfreec_plot}
plotSegments(freec)
```


## Reading everything through a single entry point

`loadCNV()` (an alias of `parseCNV()`) dispatches to the right parser based on
`cnv.method`, which makes it easy to drive the package from a manifest. The method name is
matched case-insensitively and several aliases are accepted (`freec`, `controlfreec`,
`control-freec`, ...).

```{r loadcnv}
manifest <- data.frame(
  method = c("FACETS", "SCLUST", "PureCN", "Sequenza", "FREEC"),
  file = c(
    facets.file,
    sclust.file,
    purecn.file,
    sequenza.file,
    freec.file
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

callers <- mapply(
  function(m, f) {
    obj <- loadCNV(f, cnv.method = m, sample = "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T", genome = "hg38")
    obj@sample <- "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T"
    obj
  },
  manifest$method, manifest$file,
  SIMPLIFY = FALSE
)

data.frame(
  method = sapply(callers, function(x) x@method),
  purity = sapply(callers, function(x) round(x@purity, 2)),
  ploidy = sapply(callers, function(x) round(x@ploidy, 2)),
  segments = sapply(callers, function(x) length(x@segments))
)
```

Besides the caller-specific parsers, the package can also read the generic interchange
formats (`parseSEG()`, `parseVCF()`, `parseTSV()`) and can write the harmonised object
back out with `saveSEG()`, `saveVCF()`, `exportGISTIC()` or `saveAnnotSV()`.


# Comparing all callers on the same sample

Because every parser returns the same structure, the five results can simply be put in a
list and plotted together. With more than three panels `plotSegments()` drops the
per-panel titles and identifies each track by a `sample` / `method (purity)` label in the
left gutter; `sample.label.width` controls how aggressively long sample names are
truncated.

```{r all_callers}
#| fig.height: 11
plotSegments(
  callers,
  main = "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T across five callers",
  sample.label.width = 20
)
```

The differences are striking even though the input data are identical: the estimated
purity ranges from 0.29 to 0.54 and the number of segments spans an order of magnitude.

`compareSegmentStatus()` quantifies that impression for any pair of callers.

```{r caller_agreement}
agreement <- lapply(callers[-1], function(x) {
  compareSegmentStatus(callers$FACETS, x)$stats %>%
    dplyr::mutate(method = x@method)
}) %>%
  dplyr::bind_rows()

agreement
```


# Cohort level plotting

`plotCNVFreq()` summarises a *collection* of segmentations as the frequency of gains and
losses along the genome. It expects a consensus object built by `findConsensus()`, which
first has to be given a list of objects that all cover the genome — `fillGaps()` inserts
the neutral stretches that a caller may have left out.

`findConsensus()` supports two modes, and the distinction matters:

* `ignore.samples = FALSE` — all the objects describe the **same** sample (typically the
  same tumour run through different callers). The list has to be *named*, and those names
  become the column names of the consensus matrix.
* `ignore.samples = TRUE` — the objects are treated as **different** samples, i.e. a
  cohort. Column names are taken from the `sample` slot of each object.

## Consensus of the five callers

```{r consensus}
callers.filled <- lapply(callers, fillGaps)

consensus <- findConsensus(callers.filled, ignore.samples = FALSE)
consensus
```

The consensus segments carry one column per caller plus a set of summary statistics
(`stats.mean`, `stats.median`, `stats.sd`, `stats.majority`, `stats.majority.count`,
`stats.count`).

```{r consensus_table}
head(as.data.frame(mcols(consensus@segments)), 5)
```

```{r consensus_plot}
#| fig.height: 4
plotCNVFreq(
  consensus,
  main = "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T",
  subtitle = "Fraction of callers reporting a gain / loss"
)
```

Bars above the axis count gains, bars below count losses, and the two shades distinguish
the p and q arms. By default the frequencies are computed relative to the median copy
number of each column (`ploidy = TRUE`); with `ploidy = FALSE` they are computed relative
to an absolute copy number of 2.

```{r consensus_plot_absolute}
#| fig.height: 4
plotCNVFreq(consensus, ploidy = FALSE, main = "Relative to CN = 2")
```

## A cohort built from a parameter sweep

The FACETS directory of the example data also contains the output of a grid search over
the `snp.nbhd` and `cval` segmentation parameters, one VCF per combination. Loading those
as a cohort shows which events are robust to the segmentation settings and which are an
artefact of a particular choice.

```{r sweep_load}
sweep.files <- list.files(
  file.path(root, "FACETS"),
  pattern = "csv_[0-9]+-[0-9]+\\.vcf\\.gz$",
  full.names = TRUE
)

# a subset is enough for the vignette
sweep.files <- sweep.files[1:8]

sweep <- lapply(sweep.files, function(f) {
  tag <- sub("\\.vcf\\.gz$", "", sub(".*csv_", "", basename(f)))
  obj <- parseFACETS(f, sample = paste0("nbhd-cval_", tag), genome = "hg38")
  fillGaps(obj)
})

data.frame(
  run = sapply(sweep, function(x) x@sample),
  purity = sapply(sweep, function(x) round(x@purity, 2)),
  segments = sapply(sweep, function(x) length(x@segments))
)
```

Here the objects deliberately carry different sample names, so the cohort mode of
`findConsensus()` is the right one.

```{r sweep_consensus}
sweep.consensus <- findConsensus(sweep, ignore.samples = TRUE)
sweep.consensus
```

```{r sweep_plot}
#| fig.height: 4
plotCNVFreq(
  sweep.consensus,
  main = "FACETS parameter sweep",
  subtitle = "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T, 8 segmentation settings"
)
```

The large arm-level events are recovered by every setting, while the focal calls appear in
only a fraction of the runs — exactly the kind of stability information that is lost when
a single parameter combination is reported on its own.

The same list can of course also be stacked with `plotSegments()`:

```{r sweep_segments}
#| fig.height: 11
plotSegments(sweep[1:5], main = "FACETS segmentation settings")
```
